content.prompt: Find the global minimum and maximum for $y=x^4-2x+1$ in the domain $[-2,3]$.

spec.description: Unticked axes with arrowheads at both ends; blue quartic with closed domain endpoints. Reconstructed from the printed equation.
spec.mathematics: y=x^4-2x+1 on [-2,3]; endpoints (-2,21) and (3,76); minimum at x=1/cuberoot(2).
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent supplied graph; no answer coordinates or extrema labels.

answer.short: Global minimum at $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{2}},1-\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt[3]{2}}\right)$; global maximum at $(3,76)$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=4x^3-2\\4x^3-2&=0\\x^3&=\frac12\\x&=\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{2}}\end{aligned}$$
This stationary point lies in the domain. Compare its value with the endpoint values:
$$\begin{aligned}y(-2)&=16+4+1=21\\y\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{2}}\right)&=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{2}}-\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2}}+1\\&=1-\frac{3}{2\sqrt[3]{2}}\\y(3)&=81-6+1=76\end{aligned}$$
The global minimum is $1-\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt[3]{2}}$ at $x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{2}}$. The global maximum is $76$ at $x=3$.

content.prompt: Find the global minimum and maximum for $y=5-\sqrt[3]{(x-2)^2}$ in the domain $[-10,10]$.

spec.description: Unticked axes with arrowheads at both ends; blue curve with a pointed maximum and filled endpoints. Left endpoint below the horizontal axis; right endpoint above it.
spec.mathematics: y=5-|x-2|^(2/3) on [-10,10]; cusp at (2,5); endpoint values 5-cuberoot(144) and 1.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent supplied graph; no answer coordinates or extrema labels.

answer.short: Global minimum at $\left(-10,5-\sqrt[3]{144}\right)$; global maximum at $(2,5)$.
answer.worked:
For $x\ne2$,
$$y'=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt[3]{x-2}}.$$
The derivative is never zero and is undefined at $x=2$, where the function is defined. Compare this point with the endpoints:
$$\begin{aligned}y(-10)&=5-\sqrt[3]{(-12)^2}\\&=5-\sqrt[3]{144}\\y(2)&=5\\y(10)&=5-\sqrt[3]{8^2}\\&=1\end{aligned}$$
Since $\sqrt[3]{144}>5$, the smallest value is $5-\sqrt[3]{144}$ and the largest is $5$.
The global minimum is at $\left(-10,5-\sqrt[3]{144}\right)$ and the global maximum is at $(2,5)$.

content.prompt: State the global minimum and maximum of these functions. A sketch can help.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $y=x^2,\quad -2\le x\le2$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=2x\\2x&=0\\x&=0\end{aligned}$$
Compare $f(-2)=4$, $f(0)=0$ and $f(2)=4$.
Global minimum: $0$ at $x=0$. Global maximum: $4$ at $x=\pm2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $y=5-x,\quad 0\le x\le3$

answer.worked:
$f'(x)=-1$, so the function decreases throughout the domain.
$$\begin{aligned}f(0)&=5\\f(3)&=2\end{aligned}$$
Global minimum: $2$ at $x=3$. Global maximum: $5$ at $x=0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: $y=\sqrt{16-x^2},\quad -4\le x\le4$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{-x}{\sqrt{16-x^2}}\\f'(x)&=0\quad\text{at }x=0\end{aligned}$$
Compare $f(-4)=0$, $f(0)=4$ and $f(4)=0$.
Global minimum: $0$ at $x=\pm4$. Global maximum: $4$ at $x=0$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: $y=|x|,\quad -5\le x\le1$

answer.worked:
The derivative is undefined at $x=0$, the vertex of the graph.
Compare $f(-5)=5$, $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$.
Global minimum: $0$ at $x=0$. Global maximum: $5$ at $x=-5$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: $y=\sqrt{x},\quad 0\le x\le8$

answer.worked:
For $x>0$, $f'(x)=\frac1{2\sqrt{x}}>0$, so the function increases.
$$\begin{aligned}f(0)&=0\\f(8)&=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2\end{aligned}$$
Global minimum: $0$ at $x=0$. Global maximum: $2\sqrt2$ at $x=8$.

children.label: f
children.prompt: $y=\frac1x,\quad -4\le x\le-1$

answer.worked:
$f'(x)=-\frac1{x^2}<0$ throughout the domain, so the function decreases.
$$\begin{aligned}f(-4)&=-\frac14\\f(-1)&=-1\end{aligned}$$
Global minimum: $-1$ at $x=-1$. Global maximum: $-\frac14$ at $x=-4$.

children.label: g
children.prompt: $y=3x^2-16x+5,\quad 0\le x\le4$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=6x-16\\6x-16&=0\\x&=\frac83\\f(0)&=5\\f\left(\frac83\right)&=3\left(\frac83\right)^2-16\left(\frac83\right)+5\\f\left(\frac83\right)&=-\frac{49}{3}\\f(4)&=-11\end{aligned}$$
Global minimum: $-\frac{49}{3}$ at $x=\frac83$. Global maximum: $5$ at $x=0$.

children.label: h
children.prompt: $y=\sqrt[3]{x^2},\quad -2\le x\le8$

answer.worked:
For $x\ne0$, $f'(x)=\frac{2}{3\sqrt[3]{x}}$, which is never zero. The derivative is undefined at $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(-2)&=\sqrt[3]4\\f(0)&=0\\f(8)&=4\end{aligned}$$
Global minimum: $0$ at $x=0$. Global maximum: $4$ at $x=8$.

children.label: j
children.prompt: $y=\frac1{x-2},\quad -3\le x\le3$

answer.short: No global minimum or global maximum; the function is unbounded below and above.
answer.worked:
The function is undefined at $x=2$, so its domain is $[-3,2)\cup(2,3]$.
As $x$ approaches $2$ from below, $f(x)$ decreases without bound. As $x$ approaches $2$ from above, $f(x)$ increases without bound.
Therefore there is no global minimum and no global maximum. Infinity is not an attained function value.

content.prompt: The revenue equation for a manufacturer is $R(x)=\dfrac{80x-x^2}{4}$, where $x$ is the number of units sold, in hundreds, and $R$ is the revenue, in tens of thousands.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many units must be sold to achieve maximum revenue?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dR}{dx}&=\frac{80-2x}{4}\\\frac{dR}{dx}&=\frac{40-x}{2}.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point, $\dfrac{dR}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}40-x&=0\\x&=40.\end{align*}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2R}{dx^2}=-\dfrac12<0$ throughout the domain, this gives the maximum revenue. As $x$ counts hundreds of units, $40\times100=4000$ units must be sold.

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the maximum revenue?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}R(40)&=\frac{80(40)-40^2}{4}\\R(40)&=400.\end{align*}$$
Revenue is measured in tens of thousands of dollars, so the maximum revenue is $400\times\$10\,000=\$4\,000\,000$.

content.prompt:
The cost, $C(v)$ in dollars, of a 100 km yacht journey depends on the speed $v$ of the boat in km/h.

The cost formula is given by:
$$C(v)=\frac{50000}{v}+4000+500v$$
where $v>0$.

Find the speed of the boat that will minimise the cost, and the minimum cost.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}C'(v)&=-\frac{50000}{v^2}+500\\0&=-\frac{50000}{v^2}+500\\500v^2&=50000\\v^2&=100\\v&=10\qquad(v>0).\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}C''(v)&=\frac{100000}{v^3}\\C''(10)&=100>0.\end{align*}$$
Since $C''(v)>0$ for all $v>0$, this is the global minimum. The cost is undefined at $v=0$ and grows without bound as $v$ approaches zero from above or increases without bound.
$$\begin{align*}C(10)&=\frac{50000}{10}+4000+500(10)\\C(10)&=14000.\end{align*}$$
The speed is $10\ \mathrm{km/h}$ and the minimum cost is $\$14000$.

content.prompt:
Wobbly Skateboards looked at their sales in relation to their advertising budget. They found that the relationship between sales, $f(x)$, and thousands of dollars spent on advertising, $x$, was given by
$$f(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{45x^2}{2}+450x,\qquad 10\leq x\leq40.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: What number of advertising dollars can be expected to maximise number of sales?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=x^2-45x+450\\0&=x^2-45x+450\\0&=(x-15)(x-30)\\x&=15\text{ or }30.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=2x-45\\f''(15)&=-15<0\\f''(30)&=15>0.\end{aligned}$$
Thus $x=15$ is a local maximum and $x=30$ is a local minimum.
$$\begin{aligned}f(15)&=1125-5062.5+6750=\frac{5625}{2}\\f(30)&=9000-20250+13500=2250\\f(10)&=\frac{1000}{3}-2250+4500=\frac{7750}{3}\\f(40)&=\frac{64000}{3}-36000+18000=\frac{10000}{3}.\end{aligned}$$
Comparing the stationary-point and endpoint values, the global maximum occurs at $x=40$. Since $x$ is measured in thousands of dollars, the advertising expenditure is $\$40\,000$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: What sales can be expected for that amount of advertising? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}f(40)&=\frac{40^3}{3}-\frac{45(40)^2}{2}+450(40)\\f(40)&=\frac{10000}{3}\\f(40)&\approx3333.33.\end{aligned}$$
The model predicts approximately $3333.33$ sales.

content.prompt: The displacement of a particle from the origin is given by $x(t)=2t^3-6t^2-30t$, where $x$ is metres from the origin and $t$ is time in seconds, $0\le t\le3.5$. Give rounded numerical answers to 2 decimal places where needed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the velocity and acceleration at any time $t$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\frac{dx}{dt}\\&=6t^2-12t-30\\a(t)&=\frac{dv}{dt}\\&=12t-12\end{align*}$$Velocity is in metres per second and acceleration is in metres per second squared.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the initial velocity and acceleration.

children.label: c
children.prompt: At what time is the velocity zero?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}6t^2-12t-30&=0\\t^2-2t-5&=0\\t&=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{24}}{2}\\&=1\pm\sqrt6\end{align*}$$Only $1+\sqrt6$ lies in $0\le t\le3.5$, so the velocity is zero at $t=1+\sqrt6\text{ s}\approx3.45\text{ s}$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: What is the furthest the particle travels from the origin?

answer.worked: Compare displacement at the stationary time and the domain endpoints: $$\begin{align*}x(0)&=0\\x(3.5)&=2(3.5)^3-6(3.5)^2-30(3.5)\\&=-92.75\\x(1+\sqrt6)&=-34-24\sqrt6\\&\approx-92.79\end{align*}$$The global maximum displacement is $0$ and the global minimum is $-34-24\sqrt6$ metres. Distance from the origin is $|x(t)|$, so the furthest distance is $34+24\sqrt6\text{ m}\approx92.79\text{ m}$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: During what time interval is the velocity negative?

answer.worked: $$v(t)=6(t^2-2t-5).$$The velocity–time parabola opens upwards and has roots $t=1-\sqrt6$ and $t=1+\sqrt6$. Therefore $v(t)<0$ between these roots. Since $1-\sqrt6<0$, restricting to the given domain gives $$0\le t<1+\sqrt6.$$The upper boundary is approximately $3.45$ seconds.

children.label: f
children.prompt: When is the velocity greatest in this domain? (Hint: compare the velocity at stationary points and the domain endpoints.) What was the velocity at the time, and what is the significance of this point graphically?

answer.short: At $t=3.5\text{ s}$, the greatest velocity is $1.5\text{ m/s}$. This is the global maximum at the right endpoint of the velocity–time graph; the displacement–time graph has its greatest gradient there.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{dv}{dt}&=12t-12\\12t-12&=0\\t&=1\end{align*}$$Since $\frac{d^2v}{dt^2}=12>0$, this stationary point is a minimum of velocity. Compare the stationary and endpoint values: $$\begin{align*}v(0)&=-30\text{ m/s}\\v(1)&=6-12-30\\&=-36\text{ m/s}\\v(3.5)&=6(3.5)^2-12(3.5)-30\\&=1.5\text{ m/s}\end{align*}$$The greatest velocity is $1.5\text{ m/s}$ at $t=3.5\text{ s}$. Graphically, this is the global maximum at the right endpoint of the velocity–time graph. The displacement–time graph has its greatest gradient in the domain at this time.

content.prompt: Find the global maximum and minimum values of $y=x^3-6x^2+8$ where $-1\le x\le7$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dy}{dx}&=3x^2-12x\\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=6x-12\end{align*}$$
Stationary points occur when $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}3x^2-12x&=0\\3x(x-4)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }4.\end{align*}$$
At $x=0$, $y=8$ and $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-12<0$: local maximum at $(0,8)$.

At $x=4$:
$$\begin{align*}y(4)&=4^3-6(4^2)+8\\y(4)&=-24.\end{align*}$$
Here $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12>0$: local minimum at $(4,-24)$.

Check the endpoints:
$$\begin{align*}y(-1)&=-1-6+8\\y(-1)&=1\\y(7)&=7^3-6(7^2)+8\\y(7)&=57.\end{align*}$$
Therefore the global maximum is $57$ at $x=7$, and the global minimum is $-24$ at $x=4$.

Migrating fish try to minimise the total energy used to swim a fixed distance.
Find the value of $v$ that minimises $E$. (You may assume $v>u>0$.)

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dE}{dv}&=\frac{(v-u)(3aLv^2)-aLv^3}{(v-u)^2}\\&=\frac{2aLv^3-3aLuv^2}{(v-u)^2}\\&=\frac{aLv^2(2v-3u)}{(v-u)^2}\end{align*}$$
Let $\dfrac{dE}{dv}=0$. Since $a,L>0$ and $v>u>0$, $2v-3u=0$, so $v=\dfrac{3u}{2}$.
The denominator and $aLv^2$ are positive, so the sign of $\dfrac{dE}{dv}$ is the sign of $2v-3u$. It is negative for $u<v<\frac{3u}{2}$ and positive for $v>\frac{3u}{2}$, so this is a minimum.
The minimum occurs when $v=\dfrac{3u}{2}$.

content.prompt:
The velocity of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by
$$v=8-8e^{-2t}$$
where $t$ is the time in seconds and $x$ is the displacement in metres.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the particle is initially at rest.

answer.short: $v(0)=0\text{ m/s}$, so the particle is initially at rest.
answer.worked:
Initially, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}v(0)&=8-8e^0\\&=0\text{ m/s}.\end{aligned}$$
Therefore the particle is initially at rest.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the acceleration of the particle is always positive.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\frac{dv}{dt}\\&=(-8)(-2)e^{-2t}\\&=16e^{-2t}.\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-2t}=\dfrac{1}{e^{2t}}>0$ for all $t$,
$$a=\frac{16}{e^{2t}}>0.$$
Therefore the acceleration is always positive.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Explain why the particle is moving in the positive direction for all $t>0$.

answer.short: It starts at rest and always has positive acceleration, so $v>0$ for all $t>0$.
answer.worked: The particle is initially at rest and its acceleration is always positive. Its velocity therefore increases from zero, so it moves in the positive direction for all $t>0$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: As $t\to\infty$, the velocity of the particle approaches a constant. Find the value of this constant.

answer.worked:
As $t\to\infty$,
$$e^{-2t}=\frac{1}{e^{2t}}\to0,$$
so $\dfrac{8}{e^{2t}}\to0$ and
$$v=8-\frac{8}{e^{2t}}\to8\text{ m/s}.$$
Therefore the velocity approaches $8\text{ m/s}$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Sketch the graph of the particle's velocity as a function of time.

answer.short: An increasing, concave-down curve from $(0,0)$, approaching the horizontal asymptote $v=8$ from below.
answer.worked: The graph starts at $(0,0)$, increases with decreasing gradient, and approaches the horizontal asymptote $v=8$ from below as $t\to\infty$.

content.prompt:
An open topped fish tank of volume $30\text{ m}^3$ is to be made in the shape of a rectangular prism with length $3x$ metres, width $x$ metres and height $h$ metres.
Materials cost \$20 per square metre for the base of the tank and \$35 per square metre for the sides of the tank.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that the total cost $C$ of making the fish tank is given by
$$C=60x^2+\frac{2800}{x}.$$

answer.worked:
Volume: $3x^2h=30$, so $h=\dfrac{10}{x^2}$.
Base cost: $20(3x^2)=60x^2$.
Side area: $2(3xh)+2(xh)=8xh$, so side cost $=35(8xh)=280x\cdot\dfrac{10}{x^2}=\dfrac{2800}{x}$.
$$C=60x^2+\frac{2800}{x}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Hence find the dimensions of such a tank with the least total cost.
Give your answer correct to $3$ decimal places.

answer.short: Width $\approx2.858$ m, length $\approx8.573$ m, height $\approx1.225$ m
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}C'&=120x-\frac{2800}{x^2}\\0&=120x-\frac{2800}{x^2}\\x^3&=\frac{70}{3}\\x&\approx2.858\end{align*}$$
$C''=120+\dfrac{5600}{x^3}>0$ for $x>0$, so this is a minimum.
Width $\approx2.858$ m, length $=3x\approx8.573$ m, height $=\dfrac{10}{x^2}\approx1.225$ m.

content.prompt: A closed cylindrical can of base radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm, is to be constructed to hold $250\pi\text{ cm}^3$ of volume.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that the total surface area, $A\text{ cm}^2$, of material required to make the can is given by
$$A=2\pi r^2+\frac{500\pi}{r}$$

answer.worked:
$250\pi=\pi r^2h$, so $h=\dfrac{250}{r^2}$.
$$\begin{align*}A&=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\&=2\pi r^2+2\pi r\cdot\frac{250}{r^2}\\&=2\pi r^2+\frac{500\pi}{r}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
The material for the curved side of the can costs 0.05 cents per square centimetre, and the material for the top and base costs 0.03 cents per square centimetre.
Find the least cost for the material to be used to produce this can.
Round your answer to the nearest cent.

answer.worked:
Curved side area $=\dfrac{500\pi}{r}$ and top and base area $=2\pi r^2$.
$$C(r)=0.05\left(\frac{500\pi}{r}\right)+0.03(2\pi r^2)=\frac{25\pi}{r}+0.06\pi r^2$$
$$\begin{align*}C'(r)&=-\frac{25\pi}{r^2}+0.12\pi r\\0&=-\frac{25\pi}{r^2}+0.12\pi r\\r^3&=\frac{25}{0.12}=208.3\ldots\\r&=5.93\end{align*}$$
$C''(r)=\dfrac{50\pi}{r^3}+0.12\pi$, and $C''(5.93)=1.13>0$, so this is a minimum.
$$C(5.93)=\frac{25\pi}{5.93}+0.06\pi(5.93)^2\approx19.87$$
The least cost is approximately 20 cents.

content.prompt:
A cubic function $f(x)=x(4x-x^2+3)$ has a local minimum at $x=-\frac{1}{3}$ and a local maximum at $x=3$.

Find the maximum value of the curve in the domain $[-1,5]$.

answer.worked:
Compare $f$ at the turning points and the endpoints of $[-1,5]$; both turning points lie in the domain.

Turning points:
$f(-\tfrac13)=-\tfrac13\left(-\tfrac43-\tfrac19+3\right)=-\tfrac{14}{27}$
$f(3)=3(12-9+3)=18$

Endpoints:
$f(-1)=(-1)(-4-1+3)=2$
$f(5)=5(20-25+3)=-10$

The largest value is $18$, so the maximum value on $[-1,5]$ is $18$, at $x=3$.

entries.description: Global Maxima and Minima

Mt Kosciuszko is the tallest mountain in Australia.
Mt Everest is the tallest mountain in the world.
Similarly, a turning point can be:
• A local maximum: the largest value in its neighbourhood.
• A global maximum: the largest value in its entire domain.
• A local minimum: the smallest value in its neighbourhood.
• A global minimum: the smallest value in its entire domain.

A neighbourhood in mathematics is
"the area immediately around a point"
(you will learn the formal definition in university)

To find global maxima and minima, examine and compare the function value f(x) at:
• Turning points.
• Domain boundaries.
• Discontinuities of f′(x).
